newsitem.title: BOLIVIA: SOCCER-SHOWERS AND FLAGS DOMINATE COPA AMERICA.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-SHOWERS AND FLAGS DOMINATE COPA AMERICA.

text.p: Flags and showers, rather than soccer, dominated the Copa America on Thursday.
The host nation began their campaign for a second title on home soil with a 1-0 win over lightly-regarded Venezuela, while Peru, fielding virtually an under-23 team, shocked Uruguay 1-0.

But the most intriguing action happened off the field, where a diplomatic row brewed between Bolivia and Chile after the latter claimed an altered Chilean flag had been displayed at Wednesday's opening ceremony in Cochabamba.
Chile also claimed the role of victims in the cold water controversy, which followed their 1-0 defeat by Paraguay in the opening game the same night.
They protested that there was no hot water in the dressing room, forcing players to take cold showers in a city where the altitude causes evening temperatures drop to near freezing.

In Santiago, Miguel Insulza, the Chilean government's Foreign Minsiter, said his country would make a formal complaint to Bolivia because the flag at the opening ceremony appeared without its large white star.
"This sort of thing makes the Bolivian people look bad. It's organising a sports competition being shown all over, and everyone sees these demonstrations of bad manners," he said.

Insulza did not say whether he thought the Bolivians deliberately altered the flag or if it was a careless omission. But Chile coach Nelson Acosta said he considered the incident a deliberate show of disrespect.

Bolivians have bitterly resented their neighbours to the south since the War of the Pacific in the 1880s, when the now landlocked country lost much of its territory and its outlet to the Pacific Ocean to Chile.
The Bolivian government described the incident as an "accidental human error" and said the country's football federation was a private entity over which it had no control.
"It was a mistake on the part of the Bolivian Football Federation and the organisers of the Copa America," said Mauricio Antezana, the government's official spokesman.

While the government blamed the organisers for the flag row, organisers in Cochabamba blamed the Chilean water fiasco on a burst pipe. They said the pipe under the pitch was broken during the opening ceremony.
On the pitch, the competition got off to an inauspicous start with as many sendings off as goals in first four games.
Attendances have been hugely disappointing with just 5,000 watching Peru beat Uruguay in Sucre and only 13,000 witnessing the host nation's win in the capital La Paz at 3,600 metres above sea level.
"This is soul-destroying, we didn't expect this," said Romer Osuna, president of the organising committee as he looked at the empty terraces in the capital's Hernando Silas stadium.
Lack of interest can be blamed on the decision to cram the competition between World Cup qualifiers, forcing many teams to rest their star players.

Peru took one of the most drastic measures, bringing what was virtually an under-23 team. But a goal direct from a free-kick by Martin Hidalgo stunned Uruguay, who had several seasoned internationals in their team, in a group B game.

Venezuela had conceeded 13 goals on their two previous visits to La Paz but world class goalkeeping by Rafael Dudamel kept Bolivia to one goal, scored after 60 mintues by Milton Coimbra in another group B match.
David MacIntosh of Venezuela and Juan Manuel Pena of Bolivia were sent off, while the other game saw Peru's Eddie Carazas dismissed.
Wednesday's games produced no sendings-off but only one goal -- leaving the tallies of red cards and goals both at three.

Paraguay are one of the few teams at near full strength and their fiery goalkeeper and captain Jose Luis Chilavert grabbed attention again Thursday when he said he had received an offer to play for an NFL team in the United States.

Chilavert, who regularly scores goals from free kicks and penalties and packs one of the most powerful shots in the game, displayed his skills with an American football while his teammates slogged through a training session.
